messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Sofia, a twenty-six-year-old chemistry graduate student, traced the rim of her water glass, her focus fixed anywhere but on the therapist. The story of the last eight months felt like a collection of sharp, disconnected fragments, and she struggled to find the words to string them together. It began during a late-night session in the organic chemistry lab. She was alone, pushing to finish a synthesis before a deadline. She remembers the acrid smell of acetone used for cleaning, then a different, sharper odor as a glass beaker slipped from her grasp. The crash was followed by an immediate, searing pain across her forearms and the front of her legs. Almost simultaneously, the lab’s notoriously faulty overhead lights flickered and died, plunging the windowless room into absolute darkness. All she had was the suffocating chemical smell and the feeling of fire on her skin. She can’t recall the sequence clearly—did she scream before or after she stumbled towards the emergency shower? The memory is a blur of panic, pain, and the disorienting blackness.

In the weeks that followed, after the hospital stay and the initial healing of the chemical burns, Sofia found the lab had followed her home. Her body remained on high alert, a tightly wound spring ready to snap at the slightest provocation. She felt a constant, humming tension in her shoulders and jaw, as if perpetually braced for impact. When her roommate once gently touched her back to get her attention, Sofia gasped and recoiled so violently she knocked a stack of books from her desk. This betrayal by her own body became a source of deep shame. She started to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with her, some irreparable flaw the accident had exposed. Why else would her heart hammer in her chest and sweat break out on her palms when she smelled the antiseptic cleaning solution used in the university library? She knew she was safe, but her body screamed otherwise, an enemy within that refused to stand down.

Her world began to shrink. The science building, once a place of ambition, was now a monument to her terror. She began taking a ten-minute detour around the entire quad just to avoid walking past its doors. At night, her apartment became a landscape of threats. She would wake up in the pitch-black of her room with a jolt of pure panic, her breath catching in her throat, the darkness feeling heavy and suffocating just as it had in the lab. When fragments of the memory returned, they were visceral. It wasn’t just a thought; she would feel a phantom, burning pain flare up along her forearms, a ghost of the chemical spill that was so real it made her cry out.

This constant state of threat monitoring bled into every corner of her life. In lectures, she found she couldn’t follow the professor’s arguments. Instead, her eyes would dart around the room, scanning the faces of her classmates, checking the exits, her mind cataloging potential dangers. She tried desperately to push the event away, to erase it by filling her mind with anything else—complex formulas, endless scrolling on her phone—but the effort was exhausting. The avoidance took its toll; her academic advisor recently sent a formal warning about her failure to attend mandatory lab sections for her current courses. The prospect of having to re-enter that building, or any lab, felt impossible. Sofia finally sought help because she could no longer trust her own body and feared this internal state of emergency would cost her the future she had worked so hard to build.
